Title: The Sun Never Set (Part 6 of 10): Rebellion and the Crown, 1857–1879

Summary: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 ended the East India Company and put India directly under the Crown. Over the next twenty years Britain burned the Summer Palace in Beijing, crushed the Morant Bay rebellion in Jamaica, faced Fenian risings, created the Dominion of Canada, bought into the Suez Canal, made Victoria Empress of India during a catastrophic famine, and was defeated at Isandlwana. This post covers 1857 to 1879, alongside the American Civil War, Meiji Japan and the unification of Germany.

---

## The big picture

In 1857 the Company's own Indian soldiers rose against it across northern India, and for several months British rule there was in real danger. The rebellion was suppressed with great violence, and the Company was abolished in 1858. India was now ruled by the British government through a Viceroy.

The years after 1857 saw a change in tone. The reforming, "civilising" confidence of the 1830s gave way to a harder belief in racial difference and the need for firm rule. At the same time, white settler colonies were moving towards self-government, starting with the Dominion of Canada in 1867. The empire was splitting into two different kinds of place.

## The Indian Rebellion of 1857–1858

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| Early 1857 | Rumours spread that new Enfield rifle cartridges are greased with cow and pig fat; sepoys at Barrackpore and Berhampur resist |
| 29 March 1857 | Mangal Pandey attacks officers at Barrackpore; hanged in April |
| 10 May 1857 | **Meerut**: sepoys mutiny, kill officers and civilians, march to Delhi |
| 11 May 1857 | Mutineers reach Delhi and proclaim the aged Bahadur Shah Zafar as emperor |
| June 1857 | Siege of the British at Cawnpore (Kanpur); after the surrender, massacres at Satichaura Ghat and later Bibighar |
| June–November 1857 | Siege of the Lucknow Residency; Awadh rises broadly, not just the army |
| September 1857 | British retake Delhi; widespread killing of civilians; Bahadur Shah's sons shot |
| 1857–1858 | Revenge campaigns: rebels blown from cannon, villages burned, mass hangings |
| June 1858 | Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi killed in battle near Gwalior |
| August 1858 | **Government of India Act**: the East India Company's rule ends |
| 1 November 1858 | Queen Victoria's Proclamation promises religious toleration and no further annexations |
| 1858–1859 | Bahadur Shah exiled to Rangoon; Tantia Tope captured and hanged (April 1859) |

What it is called matters. British writers long called it the "Sepoy Mutiny". Many Indian historians call it the First War of Independence. Most scholars now use "Indian Rebellion" or "Uprising", because it involved civilians, landholders and princes as well as soldiers, but was concentrated in the north and not supported everywhere. Sikh, Gurkha and many south Indian troops fought for the British.

## Main timeline (1856–1879)

| Year | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1856–1860 | **Second Opium War**, with France | In October 1860 British and French troops loot and burn the Old Summer Palace in Beijing. The Convention of Peking legalises opium and cedes Kowloon |
| 1859–1860 | Indigo revolt in Bengal | Peasants refuse to grow indigo for European planters |
| 1860–1872 | Second phase of the New Zealand Wars; invasion of the Waikato (1863) | Massive confiscation of Māori land |
| 1861 | Lagos annexed; Trent affair nearly causes war with the US | |
| 1861–1865 | American Civil War; "cotton famine" in Lancashire | Many Lancashire mill workers supported the Union despite losing work |
| 1863 | Bombardment of Kagoshima, Japan | Britain retaliates for the killing of a British merchant |
| 1864–1865 | Bhutan (Duar) War | Bhutan cedes territory |
| 1865 | **Morant Bay rebellion**, Jamaica | Over 400 killed by troops and martial law; Governor Eyre's actions split British opinion. Jamaica loses its elected assembly |
| 1866–1871 | Fenian raids from the US into Canada | Irish-American veterans attack British North America |
| 1867 | **Canadian Confederation** (1 July); Fenian Rising in Ireland | The first self-governing dominion |
| 1868 | Expedition to Abyssinia; Magdala stormed, Tewodros II kills himself | Britain withdraws afterwards, taking looted treasures |
| 1869 | Suez Canal opens | Cuts the sea route from Britain to India by thousands of miles |
| 1869–1870 | Red River Resistance led by Louis Riel | Leads to the creation of Manitoba |
| 1871 | Diamond fields at Kimberley annexed | Start of the mineral revolution in southern Africa |
| 1872 | Kuka (Namdhari) rising in Punjab | Dozens blown from cannon at Malerkotla without trial |
| 1873–1874 | Third Anglo-Ashanti War | Kumasi burned; Gold Coast becomes a colony |
| 1874 | Fiji annexed; Pangkor Treaty begins British control of the Malay states | Indian indentured labour to Fiji begins in 1879 |
| 1875 | Britain buys Egypt's shares in the Suez Canal; Perak War (1875–1876) in Malaya | The Resident J. W. W. Birch is killed |
| 1876 | Royal Titles Act | |
| 1 January 1877 | Victoria proclaimed **Empress of India** at the Delhi Durbar | While a major famine was under way |
| 1876–1878 | **Great Famine** in southern and western India | Millions die; grain exports and strict relief rules worsen it |
| 1877 | Transvaal annexed | Leads to the First Boer War in 1880 |
| 1878 | Cyprus put under British administration; Congress of Berlin | |
| 1878–1880 | Second Anglo-Afghan War | British defeat at Maiwand (July 1880); Afghanistan becomes a British-controlled buffer |
| 1879 | **Anglo-Zulu War**: Isandlwana (22 January), Rorke's Drift (22–23 January), Ulundi (4 July) | Isandlwana is the worst defeat of a British army by an Indigenous force in the era |

## Resistance: wars, risings and revolts

| Years | Who | Where | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1857–1859 | Indian Rebellion | Northern and central India | Suppressed; Company abolished |
| 1856–1860 | Qing China | China | Defeated; more treaty concessions |
| 1859–1860 | Indigo revolt | Bengal | Partly successful; an Indigo Commission is set up |
| 1860–1872 | Māori iwi, including the Kīngitanga (King Movement) | New Zealand | Defeated in war; huge land confiscations |
| 1865 | Morant Bay rebellion, led by Paul Bogle | Jamaica | Bogle and the politician George William Gordon hanged |
| 1866–1871 | Fenian Brotherhood | Canada and Ireland | Defeated |
| 1868 | Tewodros II | Ethiopia | Defeated |
| 1869–1870 | Red River Métis under Louis Riel | Canada | Manitoba created; Riel goes into exile |
| 1872 | Kuka movement | Punjab | Crushed |
| 1873–1874 | Asante Empire | Gold Coast | Kumasi burned |
| 1875–1876 | Perak Malays | Malaya | Defeated |
| 1878–1880 | Afghan forces under Ayub Khan and others | Afghanistan | Britain wins militarily but withdraws |
| 1879 | Zulu Kingdom under Cetshwayo | Zululand | Defeated at Ulundi; kingdom broken up |
| 1879 | Rampa rebellion | Andhra (Madras Presidency) | Suppressed |

## Things that happened at the same time

- **1857.** The Rebellion broke out a year before the founding of the Fenian Brotherhood in Ireland and the US, during a global financial panic, and while Britain was fighting the Second Opium War. Troops on their way to China were diverted to India.
- **1865.** Morant Bay happened six months after the end of the American Civil War. The debate over Governor Eyre in Britain, with Mill and Darwin against him and Carlyle and Dickens defending him, was partly a debate about race after American emancipation.
- **1867–1869.** In three years: Canadian Confederation, the Fenian Rising, the Meiji Restoration, the Abyssinian expedition, the Suez Canal opening and the Red River Resistance.
- **1876–1879.** The same El Niño drought caused famines in India, China and Brazil at the same time. Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India in the middle of the Indian famine.
- **January 1879.** Isandlwana and Rorke's Drift happened on the same days. Rorke's Drift became one of the most celebrated British victories, partly to distract from the disaster a few miles away.

- **Flag:** Death tolls in 1857–1858 are very uncertain. Estimates of Indian deaths, including civilians and from disease and famine linked to the fighting, range from about 100,000 to far higher figures in some recent works; I have not given a single number. The 1876–1878 famine death toll is usually given as 5.5 million to over 10 million, depending on method. Morant Bay figures come from the 1866 Royal Commission (439 killed, over 600 flogged, about 1,000 homes burned).
